paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea. These sayings aren't just good advice for getting through your week. The writer says the goal is "So that your trust may be in the LORD" (Proverbs 22:19). Every saying after that, whether it's about money, friends, dinner tables or fields, is a way of putting your trust in the right place.

Look at what he keeps warning about. Wealth "makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky" (Proverbs 23:5), so don't wear yourself out chasing it. A hot-tempered friend can teach you his ways, and a pledge for someone's debt can cost you your own bed (Proverbs 22:24-27). And the poor and the fatherless? The LORD "will take up their case" (Proverbs 22:23), and "their Redeemer is strong" (Proverbs 23:11). So you don't have to grab, rush or push, because God sees everyone, and He is the one worth leaning on.

So how do you take these in? The writer begins with "Incline your ear" and "apply your mind" (Proverbs 22:17), and he ends with "Apply your heart to instruction and your ears to words of knowledge" (Proverbs 23:12). Ear, mind, heart: the whole baker goes into this. Keep the words within you, and keep them on your lips (Proverbs 22:18). And friend, this isn't the end of the thirty sayings, so keep your apron on.
